messages.content: I want to develop a learned turbulence closure that captures bidirectional energy transfer and remains stable across unseen coarse-graining scales. The targets are below 10% energy-spectrum error against filtered direct numerical simulations at two unseen filter widths, plus bounded kinetic energy, correct mean subgrid dissipation, and intermittent backscatter.

That sets both accuracy and physical-behavior goals. The closure should represent energy transfer in both directions while remaining stable when applied at coarse-graining scales it has not seen. At two unseen filter widths, its energy-spectrum error should be strictly below 10% relative to filtered direct numerical simulations. It should also keep kinetic energy bounded, match the correct mean subgrid dissipation, and reproduce intermittent backscatter.
What does bidirectional energy transfer add to the goal?

It means the closure should not represent subgrid transfer as exclusively one-way. It needs to allow both the usual transfer toward unresolved scales and reverse transfer, or backscatter. The requirement for intermittent backscatter makes clear that those reverse-transfer events should occur episodically, rather than being absent or treated as a continuous, unrestricted input of energy.
Could it show backscatter and still get mean subgrid dissipation wrong?

Yes. Capturing individual reverse-transfer events does not, by itself, ensure the right average behavior. The goal asks for both: intermittent backscatter and correct mean subgrid dissipation. Those requirements address different aspects of the same transfer behavior.
So the mean should not be used to rule out every reverse-transfer event?

Right. An average can be correct while the transfer varies, including intermittent reversals. Conversely, allowing reversals does not establish that the average is correct. The closure needs to satisfy both conditions together.
How should I read the energy-spectrum threshold?

The stated target is an energy-spectrum error below 10% against filtered direct numerical simulations at two unseen filter widths. “Below” makes 10% a strict threshold, and the reference is the filtered simulations. The goal does not specify an error formula or an aggregation convention, so those should not be assumed from the wording alone.
Why emphasize two unseen filter widths?

The two widths make the spectral target a test of behavior at more than one coarse-graining scale not previously seen by the closure. That is distinct from showing agreement only at a familiar width. The statement does not identify the widths or claim performance at every possible unseen width.
Does unseen necessarily mean more coarsened than anything it has encountered?

No. “Unseen” says the filter widths were not seen; it does not say where they lie relative to any widths encountered before. The goal concerns behavior across such coarse-graining scales without specifying their spacing or range.
What role do the filtered direct numerical simulations play here?

They are the comparison reference for the energy spectra. Filtering matters because the comparison is made at the stated filter widths, rather than against an unspecified unfiltered spectrum. The goal gives that reference but no further details about how the simulations or comparison are constructed.
If the spectra meet the threshold, would that settle the goal?

Not on its own. The below-10% spectrum target is one requirement. Bounded kinetic energy, correct mean subgrid dissipation, intermittent backscatter, and stability across unseen coarse-graining scales remain separate requirements; spectral agreement alone does not establish them.
Does bounded kinetic energy mean the energy can never rise?

No. Boundedness does not require a monotonically decreasing kinetic energy. It requires that kinetic energy not grow without bound. That leaves room for fluctuations, including behavior associated with intermittent backscatter, without treating uncontrolled growth as acceptable.
And does reproducing backscatter mean the closure should maximize it?

No. The goal is to reproduce intermittent backscatter while maintaining correct mean subgrid dissipation and bounded kinetic energy. Producing more reverse transfer is not, by itself, evidence of success; it has to fit alongside those other conditions.
Is “correct mean subgrid dissipation” a numerical target here?

It is a stated target, but no numerical value or tolerance for the mean is supplied. The wording calls for the correct mean subgrid dissipation without specifying a particular value, sign convention, or calculation procedure.
Does the goal prescribe how the closure must be learned or stabilized?

No particular model architecture, learning procedure, or stabilization mechanism is specified. “Learned turbulence closure” identifies the kind of closure to develop, while the rest of the statement describes the behavior and comparisons it must satisfy.
I want to keep the wording clearly aspirational, not imply that the tests have passed.

Then frame these as targets: develop a learned turbulence closure that captures bidirectional energy transfer and remains stable across unseen coarse-graining scales; aim for below 10% energy-spectrum error relative to filtered direct numerical simulations at two unseen filter widths; and require bounded kinetic energy, correct mean subgrid dissipation, and intermittent backscatter. None of those targets, as stated, claims an achieved result.

As a proposed approach, train a filter-width-conditioned equivariant stress network on filtered direct numerical simulation data. It would combine mean-dissipation-calibrated eddy viscosity with energy-budget-limited stochastic backscatter.

That proposal gives the learned closure two complementary components: an eddy-viscosity contribution calibrated to mean dissipation and a stochastic contribution intended to represent backscatter, limited by an energy budget. Conditioning the equivariant stress network on filter width makes coarse-graining scale an explicit input. Training on filtered direct numerical simulations provides the proposed data source. This is an approach to pursue, not a claim that it already meets the closure’s accuracy or stability targets.
What is the stress network learning in this description?

It is a network for the stress used by the learned turbulence closure. The description says it is equivariant and conditioned on filter width, and that it combines the calibrated eddy-viscosity and budget-limited stochastic-backscatter contributions. It does not specify a network architecture, an exact stress formula, or how the contributions are parameterized.
Why include filter width explicitly?

Filter-width conditioning lets the proposed network take the coarse-graining scale into account rather than treating that scale as implicit. That is relevant to the aim of operating across unseen coarse-graining scales. It does not, by itself, establish that the closure will generalize to the two unseen filter widths in the spectrum target.
Does conditioning say how many filter widths the training data must contain?

No. The proposal identifies filter width as a conditioning input and filtered direct numerical simulations as the training data, but it does not specify the number or values of training widths. The separate target calls for evaluation at two unseen filter widths.
What does equivariant commit us to?

In general, equivariance means a model’s output transforms consistently when its input undergoes a specified transformation. Here, the proposal calls for an equivariant stress network, but it does not name the transformations or give their mathematical representation. It would be premature to attribute a particular symmetry group or construction to the proposal.
Explain the role of mean-dissipation-calibrated eddy viscosity without making it sound like a completed result.

The proposed eddy-viscosity contribution is to be calibrated with mean subgrid dissipation in mind. That connects it to the goal of obtaining the correct mean subgrid dissipation. The phrase describes an intended calibration, not evidence that the resulting closure has already achieved the correct mean.
And the stochastic backscatter component?

It is the proposed mechanism for representing intermittent reverse energy transfer. Calling it stochastic allows for variability in that contribution, while “energy-budget-limited” says its backscatter is constrained by an energy budget. The proposal does not specify a probability distribution, an event frequency, or a numerical budget limit.
Why would the backscatter need an energy-budget limit?

The limit expresses the intention to permit reverse transfer without allowing that contribution to inject energy without regard to a budget. That aligns with seeking intermittent backscatter alongside bounded kinetic energy. It is not, on its own, a demonstration that kinetic energy will remain bounded.
Is the eddy-viscosity part supposed to eliminate the stochastic part’s reversals?

No. The proposal combines the two, rather than describing one as a way to remove the other. The eddy-viscosity contribution is calibrated to mean dissipation; the budget-limited stochastic contribution represents backscatter. The intended closure still needs both appropriate average behavior and intermittent reverse-transfer events.
Should I interpret “combine” as a specific equation, such as simply adding two predicted stresses?

Not from this wording alone. It says the stress network combines those contributions, but it does not give the mathematical operation or say which quantities the network predicts directly. A particular equation would be an additional design detail.
Does training on filtered DNS mean the filtered simulations are also the comparison reference?

The proposal uses filtered direct numerical simulations for training. The goal separately specifies filtered direct numerical simulations as the reference for the energy-spectrum error at two unseen filter widths. Those are distinct roles—training data and evaluation reference—and the proposal does not specify the data split or evaluation procedure.
Can we say the proposed components address bidirectional transfer?

As an intended design, yes: the combination provides a dissipation-oriented contribution and a backscatter contribution, corresponding to the two directions of transfer the closure aims to capture. Whether it actually reproduces the required transfer behavior is something the proposal leaves to be established.
Would the energy-budget limit guarantee both correct mean dissipation and bounded energy?

No such guarantee is stated. The budget limit constrains the proposed backscatter contribution, while calibration addresses the mean-dissipation aim. The behavior of the combined closure—including bounded kinetic energy and correct mean subgrid dissipation—would still need to be assessed.
What about the below-10% spectrum-error target?

It remains a target for the learned closure: energy-spectrum error below 10% against filtered direct numerical simulations at two unseen filter widths. The proposed architecture and training source are meant to serve that broader goal, but the proposal contains no measured error and no assertion that the threshold has been reached.
Can you phrase the proposal in one sentence without turning its intended benefits into findings?

Train a filter-width-conditioned equivariant stress network on filtered direct numerical simulations, combining mean-dissipation-calibrated eddy viscosity with energy-budget-limited stochastic backscatter as a proposed way to pursue scale-aware, bidirectional transfer while retaining the closure’s accuracy and bounded-energy targets.
Can a width-conditioned energy-budget cap preserve 95th-percentile backscatter bursts without destabilizing kinetic energy at unseen filter widths?

It is possible in principle, but the question cannot be settled from the proposal alone. A width-conditioned cap could limit the energy supplied by backscatter differently at different coarse-graining scales. The challenge is to avoid suppressing the strong bursts represented by the 95th percentile while still preventing kinetic energy from growing without bound at unseen filter widths. No observed burst statistics or stability results have been given.
What does the 95th percentile add to the question?

It focuses attention on relatively strong backscatter events rather than just their average behavior or mere presence. A closure might produce occasional reverse transfer yet still underrepresent its stronger bursts. Conversely, preserving a high-percentile burst statistic would not, by itself, establish that kinetic energy remains bounded.
Does preserving those bursts mean every large event must pass through the cap unchanged?

Not necessarily. The question asks whether the cap can preserve 95th-percentile backscatter bursts, but it does not specify an event-by-event matching rule or how preservation is measured. It expresses a tension: the cap should not erase the strong intermittent behavior of interest, yet it must constrain energy input enough to avoid destabilizing kinetic energy.
Could the cap be safe simply by being very restrictive?

A highly restrictive cap might limit backscatter energy input, but that alone would not answer the question. If it clips the stronger bursts excessively, it could fail the preservation part even if kinetic energy stays bounded. Both sides need to hold together.
And if it keeps the strong bursts, is that automatically unsafe?

No. A strong intermittent backscatter event does not automatically imply unbounded kinetic energy. The issue is whether the allowed reverse transfer, considered along with the rest of the closure’s behavior, remains compatible with bounded energy at unseen filter widths. The question leaves that outcome open.
Why should the energy-budget cap depend on filter width?

Making the cap width-conditioned means its constraint can take the coarse-graining scale into account. That is relevant because the question concerns unseen filter widths, not only a single familiar scale. Width conditioning is a proposed way to adapt the constraint; it is not a guarantee that the resulting behavior will be stable or preserve burst strength there.
Would conditioning the cap on width guarantee sensible behavior between or beyond widths represented in training?

No. Supplying filter width as an input does not guarantee how the cap behaves at an unseen value. The question specifically asks whether the intended balance survives at unseen filter widths; the available description gives no result for such widths or rule that would establish it in advance.
Is this asking about the same thing as correct mean subgrid dissipation?

Not exactly. Correct mean subgrid dissipation concerns average transfer, while a 95th-percentile backscatter burst concerns relatively strong intermittent reverse-transfer behavior. The cap must also avoid destabilizing kinetic energy. A satisfactory mean would not automatically show that the upper-end bursts are preserved or that energy remains bounded.
Can the 95th percentile be interpreted as a 95% success rate?

No. A 95th percentile describes a location in a distribution of backscatter-event magnitudes under some definition; it is not a claim that 95% of runs succeed, nor a stated stability probability. The question does not specify the underlying sampling or percentile calculation, so a more exact interpretation should not be assumed.
Does the question tell us what numerical energy budget the cap should enforce?

No. It identifies an energy-budget cap conditioned on width, but gives no cap value, budget formula, or rule for applying it. It asks whether such a constraint can strike the desired balance rather than specifying a finished implementation.
If kinetic energy stays bounded, can I say the backscatter component is adequate?

Not on that basis alone. Bounded energy addresses stability, while the question also asks about preserving 95th-percentile backscatter bursts at unseen widths. A cap that achieves bounded energy by eliminating those bursts would not meet both parts of the question.
What if the bursts are preserved at one unseen width?

That would address only the width at which they were preserved. The question uses unseen filter widths in the plural, so it does not reduce to a single-width observation. It also requires that preserving the bursts not destabilize kinetic energy at those widths.
Should we assume that a particular width is the most difficult one?

No. No filter-width values or relative difficulty are supplied. The question is about whether width conditioning and an energy-budget limit can jointly maintain the desired burst behavior and bounded energy at unseen widths, without identifying which width might be most demanding.
How does this relate to the proposed stochastic backscatter?

The proposed closure includes energy-budget-limited stochastic backscatter. This question probes a specific tension within that idea: whether a width-conditioned version of the budget cap could permit strong intermittent events, represented here by 95th-percentile bursts, without compromising kinetic-energy stability when the filter width is unseen. It asks for an outcome that has not yet been established.
Can you state the question without making it sound like either outcome is already known?

Can a filter-width-conditioned energy-budget cap retain the 95th-percentile bursts of intermittent backscatter at unseen filter widths while keeping kinetic energy bounded there? That wording leaves both burst preservation and stability as open conditions.

Here is the hypothesis I want to examine: at unseen filter widths of 16η and 32η, budget-capped backscatter keeps kinetic energy below 1.2× filtered-DNS levels and 95th-percentile backscatter error below 15%.

That is a testable hypothesis, not an observed result. It makes two predictions at each unseen width, 16η and 32η: kinetic energy stays strictly below 1.2 times the filtered-DNS level, and the error in 95th-percentile backscatter stays strictly below 15%. Both conditions would need to hold to support the hypothesis as stated.
Does “below 1.2× filtered-DNS levels” mean the closure’s kinetic energy must match filtered DNS exactly?

No. It sets an upper threshold relative to the filtered-DNS kinetic-energy level, not an exact-match requirement. For a positive reference level, 1.2× corresponds to 20% above it; the prediction requires the closure’s kinetic energy to remain below that upper threshold. The wording does not state a separate lower threshold.
Is reaching exactly 1.2× enough?

No. “Below 1.2×” is strict: a value equal to 1.2 times the filtered-DNS level would not meet that stated threshold. The same reading applies to the backscatter condition: an error equal to 15% would not be below 15%.
What is the significance of naming 16η and 32η?

They identify the two unseen filter widths to which this prediction applies. The hypothesis is more specific than a general claim about unseen scales: it names 16η and 32η and sets the same kinetic-energy and 95th-percentile backscatter-error thresholds at both. It does not make a prediction for every other filter width.
Could the result at 16η compensate for missing a threshold at 32η?
Not under the hypothesis as written. It says the behavior holds at unseen 16η and 32η. Meeting both thresholds at one width would not make up for exceeding either threshold at the other.
Likewise, could a low backscatter error compensate for excessive kinetic energy?

No. The conditions are joined: the proposed budget-capped backscatter is hypothesized to keep kinetic energy below 1.2× filtered-DNS levels while also keeping 95th-percentile backscatter error below 15%. Success on one measure does not erase a failure on the other.
What does the 95th-percentile condition focus on?

It focuses the prediction on relatively strong backscatter behavior, rather than only average transfer or whether any backscatter occurs. The hypothesis assigns that 95th-percentile measure an error threshold of strictly below 15%. It does not specify how events are sampled, how the percentile is calculated, or how the percentage error is defined.
Does the hypothesis explicitly say what the backscatter percentile is compared against?

No. It explicitly names filtered-DNS levels as the reference for the kinetic-energy threshold, but does not separately state the reference or formula for the 95th-percentile backscatter error. Those details should not be silently filled in when interpreting the prediction.
Why pair a burst-related error with a kinetic-energy threshold?

The pair captures the tension being examined: budget-capped backscatter should retain strong intermittent reverse-transfer behavior without permitting too much kinetic energy relative to filtered DNS. A stringent cap might affect the bursts, while allowing bursts does not by itself establish control of kinetic energy. The hypothesis predicts that both specified thresholds can hold at 16η and 32η; it does not establish that they do.
Is this a hypothesis that all kinetic-energy trajectories are bounded for all time?

No. It predicts kinetic energy below 1.2× filtered-DNS levels at the two named unseen widths, but does not define a time interval, whether the comparison is instantaneous or aggregated, or a universal long-time bound. Those stronger interpretations are not contained in this statement.
Can we infer the exact mathematical form of the energy-budget cap from these thresholds?

No. “Budget-capped backscatter” identifies the proposed constrained contribution, but the hypothesis gives neither a cap formula nor a numerical budget. The 1.2× and 15% values are predicted outcome thresholds, not a specification of the cap itself.
Does the hypothesis assert the below-10% energy-spectrum error target too?

No. This hypothesis specifies kinetic energy and 95th-percentile backscatter error at unseen 16η and 32η. It says nothing about a measured energy-spectrum error, so its truth would not automatically establish the separate below-10% spectrum target.
Or the correct mean subgrid dissipation?

That is also not asserted here. The 95th-percentile backscatter error concerns a high-percentile feature, while mean subgrid dissipation concerns an average. Even if this hypothesis held at both widths, the mean-dissipation requirement would remain a separate question.
I want to avoid describing this as if experiments have already confirmed it.

You could say: “We hypothesize that, at unseen filter widths of 16η and 32η, budget-capped backscatter will keep kinetic energy below 1.2× the corresponding filtered-DNS levels and 95th-percentile backscatter error below 15% at each width.” That retains the strict thresholds and identifies the statement as a prediction, without implying it has been verified.
The plan is to train on filtered DNS at 8η and 24η, then test LES at 16η and 32η for spectrum error, mean dissipation, 95th-percentile backscatter, and kinetic-energy bounds.

That separates the named training widths from the named test widths. Filtered DNS at 8η and 24η supplies the planned training data; LES at 16η and 32η supplies the planned tests. At both test widths, the four stated checks are spectrum error, mean dissipation, 95th-percentile backscatter, and kinetic-energy bounds. The plan does not report any outcomes.
Are 16η and 32η unseen in this plan?

They are the test widths, distinct from the two specified training widths, 8η and 24η. In that sense, the plan tests widths not listed for training. It does not describe every possible exposure the closure might have outside this stated training-and-test arrangement.
Does the plan call for training on the LES runs too?
No. It says to train on 8η/24η filtered DNS and test 16η/32η LES. The LES runs have a testing role in this plan, not a stated training role.
Why distinguish filtered DNS from LES rather than just listing four widths?

Because the data and evaluation roles differ. The plan identifies filtered DNS at two widths as the training source, then names LES at two other widths as the setting for checking the closure’s behavior. Listing the widths without those roles would lose that distinction.
Does testing in LES tell us something different from checking a stress prediction on filtered DNS?

Conceptually, an LES test examines how the closure behaves when used in a simulation, including the resulting spectrum, transfer behavior, and kinetic energy. The plan specifies those LES checks; it does not also specify a separate stress-prediction test on filtered DNS, so that should not be added to its test list.
How does this plan address the question about a width-conditioned energy-budget cap?

The 16η and 32η LES tests put the proposed behavior at widths outside the specified training set. Checking 95th-percentile backscatter alongside kinetic-energy bounds addresses the central tension in that question: whether strong intermittent reverse-transfer events can be retained without destabilizing energy. The plan says to examine both; it does not say how the tests will turn out.
Why check the 95th percentile instead of just recording whether backscatter happens?

Merely observing some backscatter would not characterize its stronger intermittent events. The 95th-percentile check directs attention to that part of the backscatter distribution. The plan does not define the sampling procedure or percentile calculation, so it does not prescribe a more detailed statistic than the one named.
Is a 95th-percentile check a claim that 95% of the LES runs remain stable?
No. The percentile refers to backscatter, not to a success rate for simulations. Kinetic-energy bounds are a separate check in the plan.
Why include mean dissipation if we are already checking backscatter?

They describe different aspects of subgrid energy transfer. The 95th-percentile backscatter check concerns relatively strong reverse-transfer behavior; mean dissipation concerns average behavior. Testing both avoids treating a burst statistic as a substitute for the mean, or the mean as a substitute for intermittent backscatter.
And why measure spectrum error as well?

Spectrum error checks the resulting distribution of energy across scales, rather than only the transfer statistics or total kinetic energy. In this plan it is one of four LES evaluation measures at 16η and 32η. Agreement on one measure would not establish agreement on the others.
Does the plan say exactly how spectrum error is calculated?
No. It names spectrum error as a test quantity but gives no formula, aggregation rule, or measurement interval. Those details should not be inferred from the short plan.
What do kinetic-energy bounds contribute beyond the other three measurements?

They make energy control an explicit part of the LES tests. Spectrum error, mean dissipation, or a backscatter percentile alone would not show whether kinetic energy remains within the intended bounds. The plan calls for checking that behavior at both 16η and 32η, without specifying here how the bounds are measured over time.
Would bounded kinetic energy require the LES energy to fall at every instant?
No. A bound limits how large kinetic energy may become; it does not require energy to decrease monotonically. The plan calls for a bounds check, not a test of continual decline.
Do the four checks apply at each test width, or can they be pooled across 16η and 32η?

The natural reading is to test the named LES measures at 16η and at 32η. The plan does not specify a pooling or aggregation rule that would let a result at one width stand in for an unmeasured quantity at the other.
Since 16η lies between 8η and 24η, does the plan establish that its test will be easier than the one at 32η?

No. The numerical ordering is clear—16η lies between the training widths, while 32η is larger than both—but the plan gives no basis for ranking the difficulty of the two LES tests or predicting their results.
Does this plan prescribe separate models for the two LES widths?

It does not say so. It specifies training widths and test widths for the proposed closure, but does not spell out how models would be allocated across those widths. A claim about separate models would add an implementation detail not present in the plan.
Does it specify how the energy-budget cap is calculated during LES?
No. The plan identifies the training and test settings and the four quantities to assess. It does not give an equation for the cap or a procedure for applying it during the LES tests.
Can I describe the 16η and 32η measurements as results yet?

Not yet. They are planned tests. The statement commits to examining spectrum error, mean dissipation, 95th-percentile backscatter, and kinetic-energy bounds in LES at those widths; it supplies no measured values or conclusion.
Put the plan in one sentence that keeps the training–test distinction explicit.

Train the proposed closure using filtered DNS at 8η and 24η, then test it in LES at 16η and 32η, assessing spectrum error, mean dissipation, 95th-percentile backscatter, and kinetic-energy bounds at the test widths.
For the LES activity, run 20-turnover-time HIT-Re390 simulations at 16η and 32η, comparing capped and uncapped closures on spectra, mean dissipation, backscatter tails, and energy.

That specifies the simulation setting, duration, widths, comparison, and quantities to examine. The activity is to run HIT-Re390 LES for 20 turnover times at each of 16η and 32η, then compare the capped and uncapped closures using spectra, mean dissipation, backscatter tails, and energy. It does not report that the runs have been completed or what either closure produces.
Does “20-turnover-time” mean twenty separate LES runs?
No. It describes a duration of 20 turnover times, not a count of independent runs. The activity does not state how many realizations or repetitions to run.
What should we infer from HIT-Re390?

It identifies the LES setting as HIT-Re390. HIT commonly denotes homogeneous isotropic turbulence, but the activity does not define the particular Reynolds-number convention behind “Re390” or give further simulation parameters. Those details should not be supplied as though they were specified.
Are 16η and 32η training widths in this activity?

No. They are the LES widths at which the capped and uncapped closures are to be compared. The stated training widths for the proposed closure are 8η and 24η; this activity concerns LES at 16η and 32η.
Why compare capped and uncapped closures rather than examining only the capped one?

The comparison lets you examine how their observed behavior differs on the named quantities, particularly backscatter tails and energy. The activity does not predict which closure will perform better. Nor does it specify every other feature of the two closures, so the wording alone does not establish that the cap is their only difference.
Can we at least say that “capped” and “uncapped” refer to the energy-budget cap on backscatter?

Yes, in this context that is the distinction being investigated: backscatter with an energy-budget cap versus backscatter without that cap. The activity does not specify the cap’s formula or how the uncapped closure is otherwise implemented.
Does running the comparison prove that any difference was caused solely by the cap?

Not automatically. A comparison can reveal differences, but attributing them solely to the cap would depend on how the two closures and runs are controlled. This activity names the comparison and its measurements without specifying those controls or making a causal finding.
What does comparing spectra contribute?

It examines how the resulting energy distributions across scales compare in the two LES cases. That is distinct from comparing total energy or transfer statistics. The activity says to compare spectra, but does not provide an error calculation or any observed spectral agreement.
Is “energy” in the list necessarily a time-averaged kinetic-energy number?

The activity says “energy” without defining a statistic or aggregation method. Given the kinetic-energy-stability question, kinetic energy is the relevant concern, but the wording does not say whether the comparison uses a time series, an average, a maximum, or another measure. It would be too specific to assume one.
How are mean dissipation and backscatter tails different comparisons?

Mean dissipation addresses average energy-transfer behavior. Backscatter tails address the relatively strong reverse-transfer events, rather than their average alone. Comparing both can show whether behavior that looks acceptable in the mean differs in its intermittent extremes; the activity does not say what those comparisons will show.
Do “backscatter tails” necessarily mean only the 95th percentile?

No. The 95th-percentile backscatter measure is relevant to the question being examined, but “backscatter tails” is broader wording. This activity does not state that the tail comparison is limited to one percentile or define the tail statistic.
Could one closure have better backscatter tails but worse energy behavior?

That is a possible pattern the two separate comparisons could reveal, not a result stated here. The activity keeps tail behavior and energy in view together because neither alone settles whether strong backscatter can coexist with controlled kinetic energy.
Does the 20-turnover-time duration establish long-time stability?

No. It specifies the duration of these LES runs. Energy behavior over 20 turnover times can be examined in this activity, but the duration alone does not establish stability for every longer time horizon.
Should we assume the four comparisons are made at both widths?

Yes, that is the natural reading: compare capped and uncapped closures on spectra, mean dissipation, backscatter tails, and energy in the LES at 16η and at 32η. The activity does not specify a rule for combining results across the two widths.
If the capped closure looks favorable at 16η, can the 32η run be skipped?
Not while carrying out this activity as stated. It calls for HIT-Re390 LES at both 16η and 32η. A comparison at one width would leave the specified comparison at the other width unexamined.
How does this activity bear on the proposed energy-budget-cap question without answering it in advance?

It puts capped and uncapped closures into LES at the two named widths and examines both sides of the question: backscatter tails and energy behavior. Spectra and mean dissipation add complementary checks on the closure’s behavior. The activity is an evaluation, not evidence yet that the cap preserves bursts or prevents energy destabilization.
Can you restate the activity without implying that the capped closure has already passed any threshold?

Run 20-turnover-time HIT-Re390 LES at 16η and 32η, and compare capped with uncapped closures on spectra, mean dissipation, backscatter tails, and energy. The comparisons are to be made; no performance or stability outcome is asserted.

The HIT-Re390 LES results at 16η and 32η are in: the capped closure maintained energy at or below 1.12× filtered-DNS levels and backscatter P95 error at or below 11%. The uncapped closure reached 1.43× filtered-DNS energy.

Those results distinguish the capped and uncapped cases on energy. At the two stated widths, the capped LES stayed at or below 1.12 times the filtered-DNS energy level and had no more than 11% error in the 95th-percentile backscatter measure. The uncapped LES reached 1.43 times filtered-DNS energy. The figures do not give an uncapped P95 error or a separate numerical result for each width.
Does “at or below” allow the capped energy to equal 1.12×?
Yes. The reported bound is ≤1.12×, so equality is included. The same applies to the ≤11% backscatter P95 error: 11% itself is within the reported bound.
Can I say the uncapped closure reached 1.43× at both 16η and 32η?

Not from this result as worded. The comparison covers 16η and 32η, but it reports only that the uncapped closure reached 1.43× filtered-DNS energy. It does not assign that peak separately to both widths.
What exactly does P95 refer to here?

P95 denotes the 95th percentile of backscatter—the measure concerned with relatively strong backscatter events. The reported figure is an error of at most 11% for that measure in the capped LES. The result does not specify the error formula or explicitly name the P95 comparison reference.
Does the 11% number mean that 11% of events were backscatter?
No. It is a percentage error in the backscatter P95 measure, not the fraction of events exhibiting backscatter. The result supplies no event-frequency percentage.
How should I describe the energy difference without overstating what was measured?

You can say that, in the reported HIT-Re390 LES at 16η and 32η, capped-closure energy remained at or below 1.12× filtered-DNS levels, whereas the uncapped closure reached 1.43×. That preserves the distinction between a bound reported for the capped case and a level reached by the uncapped case; it does not imply that 1.43× was sustained throughout the runs.
Do these numbers also tell us how the spectra and mean dissipation compared?

No. Spectra and mean dissipation were among the quantities designated for comparison, but this result gives no values or conclusions for either. The numerical evidence here concerns energy and capped-closure backscatter P95 error.
Can the capped energy figure be read as a guarantee at other coarse-graining scales?
No. It reports behavior at 16η and 32η in the stated HIT-Re390 LES setting. It does not establish the same bound at other filter widths or in other simulation settings.
Is the uncapped case’s backscatter tail necessarily worse?

That is not specified. The result gives a backscatter P95 error for the capped closure but no corresponding uncapped error. The energy figures distinguish the two cases on energy, not on their relative P95 errors.
What is the most careful short statement of the evidence?
